sentences.text: 1. The appellants have challenged the impugned order dated 02.09.2015 passed by the Adjudicating Officer vide which FSAT No.33/16 the appellants were found to have violated the provisions u/S 26(2)(ii) of The Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006(FSS Act in short) r/w Section 3(1)(zx) of the FSS Act punishable u/S 51 of the FSS Act.

entities.label: STATUTE

sentences.text: The Adjudicating Officer imposed a consolidated penalty of Rs.Two Lacs Fifty Thousand only, for selling a substandard food product/important ingredients of so many other food articles as well as not arranging proper storage of various raw material as per the norms and regulations fixed for the same.

2. In the back drop, on 23.03.2013, Food Safety Officer(FSO in short) purchased a sample of Khoa, a food article for analysis from appellant no.1 Sh.Arun Kumar Jindal S/o Sh.Subhash Chander, M/s Bengali Sweet Corner, 3, Community Centre, Naraina Vihar PhaseI, Delhi28 where the said food article was found stored for use for human consumption.
Sh.Arun Kumar Jindal, appellant no.1 was found selling the article of food at the time of taking sample.
Before taking the sample, efforts were made to join the public witnesses but as none joined, Sh.Naubat Singh, Field Assistant was joined as a witness to the sample proceedings.
The sample consisted of 1kg of Khoa ready for use taken from an open tray having no label declaration.

Sample was taken after cuting Khoa into possible smallest pieces with the help of clean & dry knife and mixed properly with the same by rotating it into Arun Kumar Jindal vs Sh.R.P.Singh on 15 February, 2020 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/59690284/
1 clockwise, anticlockwise, up and down wards for several times in a clean and dry tray.

entities.text: Arun Kumar Jindal vs Sh.R.P.Singh on 15 February, 2020 Indian Kanoon
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: 20 drops of formalin in each sample bottle was added with a clean and dry droper.
The sample was taken as per direction of Designated Officer Sh.K.K.Mittal.
FSO divided the sample of Khoa into four equal parts then and there by putting the same into four clean and dry glass bottles.
Each part containing the sample was separately packed, fastened and sealed according to the provisions of FSS Act and Rules/Regulations 2011 made there under.

Notice in Form VA was given to Sh.Arun Kumar Jindal/Partner Incharge/Food Business Operator(FBO in short) and the price of sample was also offered to him but the same was not accepted saying that Khoa was used for preparation of sweets for sale for human consumption.
Panchnama was prepared and signed by Sh.Arun Kumar Jindal and other witness Sh.Naubat Singh, Field Assistant.
One part of the aforesaid sample of Khoa was sent to the Food Laboratory, Govt. of NCT of Delhi for analysis.

entities.text: Food Laboratory, Govt. of NCT of Delhi
entities.label: ORG

sentences.text: FBO did not request to send the fourth part of the sample for analysis from an accredited Laboratory under Rule 2.4.5 of The Food Safety and Standards Rules, 2011( FSSR in short) at the time of taking sample.
The remaining two counterparts of the sample were kept in a sealed packet and were deposited with the Designated Officer Sh.K.K.Mittal.

3. The Food Analyst vide his report no.FSS/362/2013 dated 05.04.2013 has reported that the sample is substandard because BR value exceeds the prescribed maximum limit of 43.0 and Baudouin test is positive.

The Designated Officer concerned sent copy of the Food Analyst report to the FBO and the firm M/s Bengali Sweets Corner for giving them an opportunity to file an appeal against the report of the Food Analyst.
However, no appeal was preferred.
The FSO thus filed the complaint before the Adjudicating Officer u/S 26 (2)(ii) FSS Act r/w Section 3(1) (zx) FSS Act punishable u/S 51 of FSS Act.
Notice was duly sent.

The appellants in their reply before the Adjudicating Officer took a plea that on account of Holi festival, large quantity of Khoa was purchased from the market as the sale of Khoa based sweets are on large scale during this period.
The Khoa was kept in godown alongwith other raw material like oil, vanaspati, sugar etc. and was not meant for direct sale.
The appellants submitted before the Adjudicating Officer that Khoa was ready for use for preparation of sweets etc.

It is submitted that as per Food Analyst report, the milk fat was above the minimum prescribed limit i.e. not less than 30% and the excess of BR which is 50.4(limit 40 43C) and presence of B Test shows the presence of vanaspati in Khoa.
It was submitted that as fat content was already more than the prescribed limit of 30%, thus there was no question of adding vanaspati which is usually added to make up the fat contents of Khoa.

Appellants had also taken plea that the tray and knife used by the FSO was not brought by FSO and there is a possibility that the tray and knife were already having vanaspati on it as it is a common practice that very small quantity of vanaspati is added when Burfi etc. is made so that it does not struck with the tray and while cutting the pieces so that it can come out easily.
It was further submitted that since Khoa was kept in the godown with other items, there was every possibility that traces of vanaspati has come from other sources.

The appellants also submitted that the Food Analyst did not indicate the quantity of vanaspati in the sample, therefore, it cannot be presumed that Khoa was having added vanaspati or it was in traces.

The FSO filed a reply and stated that sample article was ready for use for preparation of sweets for sale for human consumption though it was kept in store cum kitchen since Khoa(ingredient in this case) itself a food article, must conform to standards prescribed in Regulation 2.1.7(5) of The Food Safety and Standards (Food Products Standards &
Food Additives) Regulations 2011.

It was submitted that the report of the Food Analyst shows Arun Kumar Jindal vs Sh.R.P.Singh on 15 February, 2020 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/59690284/
2 presence of vanaspati in Khoa though it should have been product exclusively derived from milk or milk solids.
The FSO has stated that the knife and tray used for mixing the Khoa was clean & dry and not laced with vanaspati as stated by the respondent.

It was submitted that vegetable oil/products cannot be added in view of Regulation 2.1.1(10) of The Food Safety And Standards (Prohibition And Restrictions on Sales) Regulation 2011 which states that person shall sell milk products(like Khoa etc.) specified in Food Safety and Standards (Food Products Standards & Food Additives)
Regulation 2011 containing a substance found in milk except as provided in regulation.

It is the duty of FBO to follow guidelines regarding storage of raw materials/finished products as mentioned in schedule 4 of The Food Safety and Standards(Licensing & Registration of Food Businesses) Regulations 2011 and the appellants should not have stored Khoa with materials like oil, vanaspati, sugar etc.

sentences.text: 4. The Adjudicating Officer after taking into account the complaint, reply and the submissions of the parties found that the appellants violated the provisions u/S 26(2)(ii) FSS Act r/w Section 3(1)(zx)FSS Act punishable u/S 51 FSS Act.
Aggrieved by this, the appellants challenged the impugned order.

It was submitted that the Adjudicating Officer did not appreciate the law u/S 38(2)
FSS Act according to which the sample of food article by the FSO can only be lifted when the food article is either for sale or the same is stored for future preparations of other finished products.

In the present case, Khoa was neither for sale nor the same was under storage conditions as raw material godown and the same admittedly ready for use and therefore already in process of making sweets.
The appellants also submitted that the FSO was not empowered to take the sample of Khoa in process area.
It was further submitted that there are no standards of sweets(being prepared foods) and therefore, sweets can be made in any cooking medium including vanaspati.

The appellants also submitted that the Baudouin test can always come positive even with traces of vanaspati present in the khoa on being handled by workers and also while taking sample, FSO demanded knife and tray from the appellants which were provided but were not cleaned and dried by the FSO as required for accurate sampling as the Khoa was required to be tested minutely as per FSS standards.

Ld.Counsel for the appellants also submitted that the order of the Adjudicating Officer is liable to be set aside on the ground that the sample of Khoa was taken which was not meant for sale and nor it was stored, secondly, the sample was not taken properly and thirdly, the Food Analyst report did not indicate quantity of percentage of vanaspati in the sample.

In support of his contention, Ld.Counsel for the appellants placed reliance upon Md.Nabijan Vs State & another,
2000(1) FAC 29, Hon'ble Calcutta High Court, Rupak Kumar Vs State of Bihar & Another, 2014(1)
FAC 198, Hon'ble Supreme Court, M/s Sakthi Arrkay Traders & Caterers Private Ltd. Vs The Food Safety Officer & Others, 2015(2) FAC 4 Madras High Court, Mahalaxmidevi Flavours Pvt.Ltd. Vs Commissioner (Food Safety), Government of NCT of Delhi, 2015(2) FAC 11 Hon'ble Delhi High Court, M/s Cargill India Private Limited Vs State of Uttarakhand and Others, 2016(1) FAC 416,
Hon'ble Uttarakhand High Court.

sentences.text: 5. Per contra, Ld.Chief PP for respondent submitted that the FSO has picked up the sample in accordance with the rules and all possible precautions were taken.

He further relied upon Rule 2.1.1(10) The Food Safety And Standards(Prohibition And Restrictions on Sale) Regulations, 2011 which provides as under: "2.1.1 Notwithstanding the provisions of 2.7 of labelling and packaging regulations no person shall either by himself or by any servant or agent sell (10) milk or a milk Arun Kumar Jindal vs Sh.R.P.Singh on 15 February, 2020 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/59690284/
3 product specified in Food Safety and Standards(Food Products Standards and Food Additives)
Regulations,2011 containing a substance not found in milk, except as provided in the regulations."

sentences.text:
6. Ld.Chief PP for respondent has also relied upon Section 26(1) FSS Act which reads as under:
"26. Responsibilities of the food business operator.

(1) Every food business operator shall ensure that the articles of food satisfy the requirements of this Act and the rules and regulations made thereunder at all stages of production, processing, import,
distribution and sale within the businesses under his control."
7. In respect of Section 38 FSS Act, Ld.Chief PP for respondent has submitted that the FSO was duly empowered to take the sample as the same was being used for preparation of sweets.

8. Hon'ble Supreme Court in Raj Kumar Vs. State of Uttar Pradesh, (2019) 9 SCC 427 interalia held as under: "7.We are of the considered view that once standards are laid down by the legislature then those standards have to be followed.

entities.text: Raj Kumar Vs. State of Uttar Pradesh, (2019) 9 SCC 427
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
In items like milk which is a primary food, under the Act,
it is not necessary to also prove that the food item had become unfit for human consumption or injurious to health.
In cases of food coming under the Act, it is not required to prove that article of food was injurious to health.
In this case, the only question to be determined is whether the article complies with the standards laid down or not?
If it fails to comply with the standards then it will have to be treated as an adulterated article even if it is not rendered injurious to health.
Even marginal deviation from the prescribed standard cannot be ignored."

9. The bare perusal of this judgment makes it clear that Hon'ble Supreme Court has laid down in unequivocal terms that the provisions of FSS Act, 2006 and its rules and regulations have to be complied with strictly.
Even a marginal deviation will invite the penalty.
The 'Khoa' itself is a food article and is bound to comply with the standards.

As per Section 26 of the FSS Act, 2006, the FBO is under an obligation to ensure that food satisfies the requirements of this Act and the rules and regulations, even if it is in the process of processing.
10. In regard to the method of taking sample, the appellant has simply been taking a plea that there might be traces of Vanaspati on the knife and tray.
However, I consider that this plea does not have any force.

Firstly, because mere hypothesis cannot displace the case of the prosecution, secondly,
the appellant could have taken this care while the sample was being taken.
He could have insisted that knife and tray are properly cleaned.
It is not the case of the appellant that despite his asking, the knife and tray were not cleaned.
The plea that percentage of Vanaspati has not been indicated in the report will also not help, as even a marginal deviation is sufficient to attract the penalty.
11. I have carefully gone through the judgments cited by Ld.
Counsel for the appellant and the same are respectfully distinguished on the facts and circumstances of the case.
12. In view of the above facts and circumstances, I do not see any illegality in the impugned order dated 02.09.2015 passed by the Adjudicating Officer.
Hence, the appeal is dismissed.
